title: Phulkari, stitched flowers
hook: Punjab's flower-embroidered shawls, made by women and given at weddings

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sikh architecture: domes, small pavilions, pools, and doors on every side. Your line was open on all sides. Which door did you hold open? Day one thousand three hundred fifty.

A wedding morning in a Punjabi home. The bride sits very still while her mother lifts a heavy shawl out of a trunk and unfolds it over her shoulders. The cloth underneath is rough, hand-spun cotton, a deep red. But you can barely see it. Almost every inch is covered in silk thread, golden and orange and white, laid down in tiny straight stitches that catch the light and turn it into a field of flowers. Someone in the family made this, slowly, over a long time, for this morning. Today's word is that shawl.
screen: `A TRUNK OPENED ON A WEDDING MORNING.` → `ROUGH COTTON, BRIGHT SILK.` → `A FIELD OF FLOWERS.`

segments.voice: First, what it is. Phul is the Punjabi word for flower, and a phulkari is flower work: a shawl or head cloth embroidered in bright silk floss on hand-spun cotton. When the stitching covers the whole cloth, so the cotton disappears beneath it, people call it a bagh, a garden. Second, how it's made. Phulkari is worked largely from the back of the cloth, counting threads, in long darning stitches that lie flat and shine on the front. There's no pattern drawn for some designs; the pattern lives in the maker's head and hands. That's slow work, done in the gaps of a day, often with other women sitting close, talking. Third, what it carries. Phulkari belongs to Punjab's women across faiths, Sikh, Hindu and Muslim. Tradition in some families says a grandmother starts a bagh when a granddaughter is born, to give at her wedding. Whether or not a family keeps that custom, the shawl comes out at the big moments: weddings, births, celebrations. Fourth, why it sits in this path. In the Asa di Var, Guru Nanak speaks up for women. In paraphrase: why call her lesser, she from whom kings are born? A phulkari is women's work and women's wisdom, made by hand and handed down. It honors the ones who made it, the ones who wear it, and the long line between them. It's a story told without words, stitch by stitch: stitched flowers.
screen: `PHUL: FLOWER. BAGH: A GARDEN.` · `WORKED FROM THE BACK, BY COUNT.` · `GIVEN AT WEDDINGS AND BIRTHS.` · `WHY CALL HER LESSER?` · then, large: `STITCHED FLOWERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at embroidery closely. Settle, and breathe. If there's any stitched cloth near you, a cushion, a scarf, a hem, a picture of a phulkari, hold it or look at it close up. Follow one thread with your eyes. Notice how many tiny decisions sit in a single flower. If nothing is near, think of something made by hand for you, by someone who took their time. Breathe in, and stay with that patience for a while. The bell holds the time.
Phulkari. Flower work: Punjab's shawls embroidered in bright silk on hand-spun cotton, made by women and given at weddings and births. Today's word.
Your line: stitched flowers. Today, thank one woman in your life for something she made or did slowly, carefully, without being asked. Day one thousand three hundred fifty.

howItsDone: Phulkari shawls and baghs are embroidered by Punjabi women and brought out for weddings, births and celebrations; some families keep old ones as heirlooms, and the craft is still taught.
